content.title: Reload and fresh fetch confirm the upgraded Pro plan
content.intent: Prove that after a successful dashboard upgrade, a new account read and a page reload both reflect the persisted `pro` plan rather than stale client state.
content.technique_notes: Applied State / flow to the post-upgrade sequence and Persistence / refresh to the reload proof. Applied Equivalence partitioning to keep the source-defined eligible partition (`free`→`pro`) and to defer the unspecified already-`pro` partition to gap-1. No covering array was needed because the use-case exposed no independent input dimensions to combine; the risk-judged interaction strength would otherwise be 3 because the flow changes paid-plan entitlement.

content.title: Free account upgrades to Pro from the dashboard
content.intent: Prove that an eligible Free account can trigger the dashboard upgrade in place, receive same-view success confirmation, and complete the change with no payment-processing step.
content.technique_notes: Applied Equivalence partitioning to the source-defined eligible account partition (`free` can upgrade, target plan is `pro`). Applied State / flow to the in-dashboard action sequence and Negative / error to the forbidden payment-step promise. No covering array was needed because there were no independent user inputs or roles to combine; the risk-judged interaction strength would otherwise be 3 because the flow changes paid-plan entitlement.

judgements.rationale: [value_score] Ranked highest because persisted-plan confirmation on fresh fetch and reload is the core durability risk; a UI-only success signal could mask a failed entitlement write.

[value_score] Ranked second because in-place success feedback and the absence of a payment detour are user-visible promises, but they are slightly less business-critical than confirming the durable server-side plan state.
